7:5.text: That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.

provenance.other: ‘shaken in mind’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘moved away from the hope’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Colossians 1:23). Neither phrase is reproduced here; only the verb is shared.
provenance.significance: Both Pauline verses set the same three terms in the same relation — a deceiver, a doctrine about the day of Christ, and a hearer who must not be shaken or moved from the faith. Jacob 7:5 sets Sherem's hope against Jacob's steadiness in exactly that frame, and Sherem's doctrine is specifically that there is no Christ to have a day.

7:5.note: 'He had hope to shake me from the faith … wherefore, I could not be shaken.' The verbal contact is one word, but the configuration is Paul's: 2 Thessalonians 2 is the KJV's set-piece about a deceiver who tries to shake believers loose over a claim about the day of Christ, and 2:3 immediately adds 'let no man deceive you by any means' — which is what 7:18 says happened to Sherem himself. Recorded low because 'shake' and 'faith' are common and the case rests entirely on situation.
7:5.whyNot: 'Shaken' is a common KJV verb and 'the faith' as an object is Pauline boilerplate. Nothing distinctive is reproduced, and a reader who declines this link loses nothing from the chapter's argument.

7:6.text: But this I confess unto thee, that after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets:

provenance.other: ‘which they call’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the pronoun in the second person — 'that which ye call the Gospel' — because the speaker is the accuser rather than the accused.
provenance.significance: Acts 24:14 is Paul's answer to Tertullus before Felix, and the whole shape of the Sherem dispute is in it: a movement named contemptuously by its opponents, a charge of abandoning the law, a defence that appeals to what is 'written in the law and in the prophets', and a speech that opens 'this I confess unto thee'. Jacob 7 distributes those four elements across four speeches — Sherem's charge here, Jacob's appeal to the prophets at 7:11, and Sherem's own 'but I confess unto God' at 7:19, where the confession has changed sides.

7:6.note: 'Preaching that which ye call the Gospel, or the doctrine of Christ.' The KJV's only 'which they call' is Paul conceding his opponents' name for his movement, and the construction here does the same work from the accuser's end. What makes the borrowing worth recording is that the accusation Sherem then brings in 7:7 — perverting the right way and not keeping the law of Moses — is the accusation brought against Paul in Acts 21:21 and 24:5-6, and answered in this verse.

7:7.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: ‘pervert the right ways’ (the KJV's own plural) occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10 — the exact string 'pervert the right way', singular, occurs nowhere in the KJV, since Acts 13:10 itself reads 'ways'. ‘the right way’ alone occurs in four verses, of which 2 Peter 2:15 ('which have forsaken the right way') is the nearest competitor; only Acts 13:10 has the verb, and only there as 'ways'. The Book of Mormon has the singular 'way' against the KJV's 'ways', and 'of God' against 'of the Lord'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's hinge, and it turns on who is speaking. In Acts 13:10 the sentence is Paul's, addressed to Elymas the sorcerer at Paphos, and it is followed at once by the hand of the Lord falling on Elymas so that he is struck blind. Here the same sentence is Sherem's, addressed to Jacob — the accusation is running backwards. Eight verses later the Acts outcome arrives anyway, on the man who borrowed the accusation: 'the power of the Lord came upon him, insomuch that he fell to the earth'. The Book of Mormon's first anti-Christ episode gives the anti-Christ Paul's words and Elymas's fate.

7:7.note: 'Ye have led away much of this people, that they pervert the right way of God.' Four words verbatim from the KJV's sole occurrence, and far below Skousen's threshold — this is not one of his quotations. The catalogue has adjudicated the same source once already at 1 Nephi 13:27, where seven words are reproduced; a new book and a new hand, so the row is written out again here rather than deferred, per the exclusion rule for repeats across a book boundary. Note also that Acts 13:10's next clause, 'thou child of the devil', reappears in Jacob's reply at 7:14: 'because thou art of the Devil'. Two halves of one verse, seven verses apart, on opposite sides of the argument.

7:8.text: And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.

provenance.other: ‘not able to resist’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse; ‘confounded the Jews’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Acts 9:22). Neither phrase is reproduced verbatim, so the link is carried by the pairing of poured-out spirit with a disputant silenced.
provenance.significance: Acts supplies both halves of this sentence from two disputation scenes: Stephen, whose opponents cannot resist the spirit by which he speaks, and Saul at Damascus, who 'confounded the Jews … proving that this is very Christ'. The proposition Jacob confounds Sherem over is the same one — that there is a Christ — and 'confound' is Acts's word for winning that particular argument.

7:8.note: 'The Lord God poured in his spirit into my soul, insomuch that I did confound him in all his words.' The KJV does not say 'poured in' — it pours out (Joel 2:28, Acts 2:17) — and the odd preposition is the Book of Mormon's. What is KJV is the consequence: in the New Testament, a man filled with the Spirit in a dispute leaves his opponent unable to resist, and the verb for the outcome is 'confound'.

7:9.text: Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son.

provenance.other: ‘he is antichrist’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘denieth the Son’ occurs in exactly one (1 John 2:23). The Book of Mormon reproduces neither; it reproduces the definition.
provenance.significance: 1 John 2:22 defines the antichrist by a single test — denying that Jesus is the Christ — and yokes that denial to lying: 'who is a liar but he that denieth'. Jacob 7 stages the definition as a scene. The question at 7:9 is the test administered in the second person, 'Deniest thou the Christ?'; and at 7:19 the same man supplies the other half of the verse in his own voice, 'I have lied unto God: for I denied the Christ'. The episode is usually read as the Book of Mormon's first anti-Christ narrative, and the word is not in the Book of Mormon — it is in the source that supplies the test.

7:9.note: 'Deniest thou the Christ which should come?' The interrogative form is the Book of Mormon's, but the criterion is 1 John's, and Sherem answers it exactly: 'I know that there is no Christ, neither hath been, nor never will be' — a denial in all three tenses. 1830's 'nor never will be' is a double negative that 1920 corrected to 'nor ever will be'; the first edition's Sherem is the more emphatic denier.

7:11.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: ‘they which testify’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘search the scriptures’ occurs in exactly one — the same verse. The two halves of John 5:39 are the two things Jacob 7 does with the scriptures, twelve verses apart.
provenance.significance: John 5:39 is Jesus telling opponents that the scriptures they trust are witnesses against their position, and Jacob 7:10-11 runs the same move as a two-step interrogation: 'Believest thou the Scriptures?' — 'Yea' — 'Then ye do not understand them; for they truly testify of Christ.' The metalepsis is in the outcome. In John the opponents do not yield; here they do, and 7:23 closes the episode with the verse's first clause fulfilled — 'they searched the Scriptures, and hearkened no more to the words of this wicked man'. The chapter ends by obeying the imperative it began by arguing about.

7:11.note: 'They truly testify of Christ … none of the prophets have written, nor prophesied, save they have spoken concerning this Christ.' The only KJV verse in which scripture 'testifies' of Christ is John 5:39, and it is also the only one that commands searching it. Below any quotation threshold — the shared material is a clause's worth of content words, not a reproduced clause — but the pairing of the two halves across the episode is hard to get accidentally.

7:13.text: Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee.

provenance.other: ‘shew me a sign’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Judges 6:17, Gideon's request, which is granted. ‘we would see a sign’ occurs in exactly one, and ‘seeketh after a sign’ occurs in exactly two, Matthew 12:39 and 16:4, where the request is refused. 1830 prints 'Shew' and 1920 modernized it to 'Show', so the first edition sits on the KJV spelling.
provenance.significance: The whole of Matthew 12 is behind this chapter, and behind it in order. The sign demand at 12:38 is preceded seven verses earlier by the saying about the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost that shall not be forgiven (12:31) — and Sherem demands his sign specifically 'by this power of the Holy Ghost', then dies at 7:19 fearing he has committed the unpardonable sin. Read forward, Matthew 12 gives Jacob 7 its demand; read backward from 7:19, it gives the demand its penalty. Neither text makes the connection explicit.

7:13.note: 'Shew me a sign by this power of the Holy Ghost, in the which ye know so much.' The KJV has exactly two registers for asking a sign: Gideon's, which is answered, and the scribes' and Pharisees', which is refused as the mark of an evil and adulterous generation. Jacob's reply at 7:14 puts the request in the second register — 'what am I, that I should tempt God' — and the sign he finally allows is not a demonstration but a judgment.

7:14.text: Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.

provenance.other: ‘not my will’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon keeps Luke's adversative — 'Nevertheless, not my will be done' — and then restates the whole clause in reverse at the end of the verse, 'And thy will, O Lord, be done, and not mine'. ‘Thy will be done’ standing alone occurs in three KJV verses, Matthew 6:10, Matthew 26:42 and Luke 11:2.
provenance.significance: Jacob answers a demand for a sign with the sentence Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and the borrowing is doubled: Luke's order first, then the mirror. Recover the context and the submission is being made about a death — in Luke, the speaker's own; here, the hearer's. Jacob declines to name what the sign will be ('if God shall smite thee'), and the verse he declines it in is the verse in which the cup is not removed.

7:14.note: 'Nevertheless, not my will be done; but if God shall smite thee, let that be a sign unto thee.' Six words of the KJV's only 'not my will', with the adverb Luke uses to introduce it, and then the same clause inverted. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations, but the doubling is not the sort of thing a shared idiom produces.

7:14.text: Then said Paul unto him, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?

provenance.other: ‘God shall smite thee’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘a sign unto thee’ is 1 Samuel 2:34's, where the sign given to Eli is the death of his two sons in a single day.
provenance.significance: Acts 23:3 is Paul before the council, answering a man who is judging him by a law he is himself breaking — the same charge Sherem brings at 7:7, that Jacob keeps not the law of Moses. The man Paul says it to is the high priest Ananias, and five verses after Jacob says it the sign arrives in the form Acts 5 gives it: the other Ananias, who lied unto God and gave up the ghost. Two Ananiases stand behind the death of Sherem, and the chapter uses both.

7:14.note: 'But if God shall smite thee, let that be a sign unto thee that he hath power.' Four words verbatim from the KJV's only occurrence, in a scene of the same kind — a prophet answering a legal accusation with a prediction of divine violence. The second clause reaches for 1 Samuel 2:34, the KJV's model of a sign that consists in someone's death; there, as here, the sign is granted to a man who will not survive it.

7:14.text: And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.

provenance.other: ‘all power is given unto me’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘in heaven and in earth’ occurs in exactly two, Daniel 6:27 and Matthew 28:18; Daniel's is 'signs and wonders in heaven and in earth', which is the other thing this verse is about.
provenance.significance: The sign Jacob will allow is to prove two things, 'that he hath power, both in Heaven and in Earth; and also, that Christ shall come'. Matthew 28:18 is the verse in which those two propositions are one proposition, spoken by the risen Christ. Sherem asked for a sign of the Holy Ghost's power and is offered instead the terms of the Great Commission, which is what the chapter has been arguing about since 7:2.

7:14.note: 'That he hath power, both in Heaven and in Earth.' The KJV joins heaven and earth in this exact form twice, and only Matthew 28:18 makes the pair a claim about power belonging to someone. That Daniel 6:27 — the other occurrence — is about signs and wonders is a coincidence worth noting rather than pressing.

7:14.text: And Moses said unto God, Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?

provenance.other: ‘Who am I, that I should’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon substitutes the interrogative — 'What am I, that I should tempt God' — which is not in the KJV at all; the syntax is Exodus's and the pronoun is not.
provenance.significance: The dispute Sherem picked was about the law of Moses, and Jacob's demurral is made in the sentence Moses speaks at the burning bush. The metalepsis cuts against Sherem twice over: Exodus 3 is the passage in which the God of the fathers gives Moses signs precisely because he will be disbelieved, and it is the passage in which the law's own giver protests his unfitness. The man accused of converting the law of Moses into the worship of another being answers in Moses's words.

7:14.note: 'What am I, that I should tempt God to shew unto thee a sign?' Five words in the KJV's only occurrence of the construction, with the pronoun changed. The machine stream found this one and ranked it first in the verse; the payoff is that the verse it comes from is the one in which God answers the objection by handing over signs.

7:15.text: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?

provenance.other: ‘and he fell to the earth’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse; ‘fell to the earth’ without the conjunction occurs in exactly three, Joshua 7:6, 2 Samuel 1:2 and Acts 9:4, and only the last is an involuntary collapse under divine power. The machine stream ranked 2 Samuel 1:2 first here, which is a man doing obeisance.
provenance.significance: Two Acts stories end with a persecutor of the gospel struck down: Saul on the Damascus road, who falls to the earth and rises converted, and Elymas at Paphos in Acts 13:11 — the verse immediately after the one Sherem quoted at 7:7 — who is struck blind and dies out of the narrative. Sherem gets both. He falls like Saul, is nourished for many days like Saul in the house of Judas, and confesses; and he dies, like the sorcerer whose accusation he borrowed.

7:15.note: 'The power of the Lord came upon him, insomuch that he fell to the earth.' The KJV's one instance of the exact clause is Saul's. What makes the borrowing legible is the sequel: 'he was nourished for the space of many days', which is the Damascus interval of Acts 9:9-19 — three days without sight, then food — compressed into a phrase that occurs nowhere in the KJV.

7:19.text: Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.

provenance.other: ‘blasphemy against the Holy Ghost’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘shall not be forgiven unto men’ occurs in exactly one — the same verse. ‘the unpardonable’ occurs in no KJV verse: the term is post-biblical English theology, and its presence here is a datable idiom rather than a borrowed phrase.
provenance.significance: The chapter has already used Matthew 12 once, at the sign demand of 7:13, and this is the same chapter's other half. Sherem's sin is defined by Matthew's two conditions in Matthew's order: he spoke against the Holy Ghost, having demanded a sign 'by this power of the Holy Ghost', and he did so knowing better — 'the thing which thou knowest to be true' (7:14). Note also what Sherem does not say. He does not say he has blasphemed; he says he has lied. The doctrine is Matthew's, the vocabulary is a nineteenth-century pulpit's, and the two are welded in one sentence.

7:19.note: 'I fear lest I have committed the unpardonable sin, for I have lied unto God: for I denied the Christ.' Nothing is reproduced verbatim — 'unpardonable sin' is not KJV English at all — but the sin so named exists in exactly one place in the Bible, and Jacob 7 has been building the conditions for it since 7:9. Sherem's own account of his case runs the two halves of 1 John 2:22 together, the liar and the denier, and lands on the Matthew 12 verdict.

7:19.text: Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.

provenance.other: ‘lied unto men, but unto God’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has 'I have lied unto God' twice in this verse; the contiguous string 'lied unto God' occurs in no KJV verse, because in Acts the words are separated by the antithesis.
provenance.significance: Peter's sentence to Ananias is the Bible's only instance of lying to God as a nameable offence, and it is followed immediately by Acts 5:5: 'And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost.' Jacob 7:19-20 reproduces that sequence exactly — the confession of having lied unto God, then the giving up of the ghost in the next verse — and 7:21 adds the crowd's reaction that Acts 5:5 and 5:11 supply. Sherem does not merely die; he dies Ananias's death, in Ananias's order, having named Ananias's sin.

7:19.note: 'For I have lied unto God … And because that I have thus lied unto God.' Doubled, and there is exactly one biblical model for it. What raises the link from vocabulary to structure is 7:20: the man who has just said Ananias's offence dies in Ananias's next verse. The 1830 'because that I have thus lied' keeps a KJV conjunction that 1920 deleted.

7:20.text: And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things.

provenance.other: ‘gave up the ghost’ occurs in exactly 10 KJV verses and settles nothing by itself; the machine stream proposed Genesis 25:17, Ishmael's death in a genealogy. What picks Acts 5:5 out of the ten is the preceding verse: this is the only one of the ten where the man who gives up the ghost has just been told he lied unto God.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:5 has three movements — words heard, a body fallen, and fear spreading through the hearers — and Jacob 7:20-21 has the same three in the same order, with 'they were astonished exceedingly' standing where Acts has 'great fear came'. Both scenes then close on the community rather than the corpse.

7:20.note: 'When he had said these words, he could say no more; and he gave up the ghost.' A common KJV idiom, catalogued here only because 7:19 has already fixed the source. Adjudicated at moderate rather than high on that dependence: the phrase alone would not carry the link, and the row exists so that a reader arriving at 7:20 is shown the Ananias sequence rather than the ten-verse formula.

7:21.text: And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.

provenance.other: ‘great fear came’ occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 5:5 and Acts 5:11, both in the Ananias episode. ‘astonished exceedingly’ occurs in no KJV verse; the nearest KJV formations are Mark 10:26's 'astonished out of measure' and Matthew 19:25's 'exceedingly amazed'.
provenance.significance: Acts 5 gives the crowd's reaction twice, at 5:5 and again at 5:11 after the second death, and both times the community is what the narrative ends on. Jacob 7:21 does the same and then converts it: the fear becomes 'the power of God came down upon them, and they were overcome', and by 7:23 'peace, and the love of God, was restored again among the people'. The Book of Mormon takes Acts's terrifying ending and gives it a reconciliation Acts does not have.

7:21.note: 'They were astonished exceedingly; insomuch, that the power of God came down upon them.' No phrase is borrowed — the reaction word is the Book of Mormon's own — but the placement is Acts's: the onlookers' collapse is the third beat of a sequence whose first two beats (7:19, 7:20) are Acts 5:4-5. Recorded as an echo because the case rests on sequence rather than wording.

7:22.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.

provenance.other: ‘heard my cry’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘answered my prayer’ occurs in no KJV verse and is not biblical English. The address 'my Father which was in Heaven' is Matthew's formula — ‘Father which is in heaven’ occurs in fourteen KJV verses, all of them in Matthew — put in the past tense and the first person singular.
provenance.significance: Jacob's one-sentence thanksgiving is assembled from two registers that do not otherwise meet: the psalmist's 'he heard my cry' and the Sermon on the Mount's 'my Father which is in heaven'. The result is a pre-exilic Nephite giving thanks in a Matthean address for the answer to a psalm's petition, and the tense shift — 'which was in Heaven' — is the Book of Mormon's own.

7:22.note: 'For he had heard my cry, and answered my prayer.' Half the sentence is Psalm 40:1's only-occurring clause; the other half is Matthew's most repeated address. Recorded at moderate because neither piece is long, and flagged because the combination is the interesting fact, not either component.

7:23.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: ‘search the scriptures’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the past indicative where John has the imperative.
provenance.significance: The argument for this source is made at 7:11 and not repeated here. What 7:23 adds is the completion: the imperative half of John 5:39 is carried out by the people whom the testifying half had been quoted against.

7:23.note: 'They searched the Scriptures, and hearkened no more to the words of this wicked man.' The chapter's second borrowing from John 5:39, taking the clause it left behind at 7:11. Given a row of its own rather than folded into a recurrence note because the verbal match is here and a reader meeting 'searched the Scriptures' should be shown where it comes from.

7:24.text: Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end:

provenance.other: ‘perpetual hatred’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse; ‘eternal hatred’ occurs in none. The Book of Mormon substitutes its own adjective for Ezekiel's, which is why the phrase does not show in any n-gram stream.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 35 is the oracle against Mount Seir, and the hatred it names is a brother's: Edom is Jacob's twin, and the charge is that he kept his enmity against Israel in perpetuity and shed his brother's blood by the sword. Amos 1:11 makes the kinship explicit — 'he did pursue his brother with the sword'. Jacob 7:24 says the same thing of the Lamanites in one clause: 'an eternal hatred against us, their brethren', with the arms and the bloodshed attached. The Nephite–Lamanite quarrel is being written in the KJV's vocabulary for the Edom quarrel, by a narrator named Jacob.

7:24.note: 'They delighted in wars and bloodsheds; and they had an eternal hatred against us, their brethren.' No phrase is reproduced — 'eternal' for 'perpetual' — but the Bible names a hatred of this kind exactly once, and it is a hatred between brothers who are also nations, which is what the Book of Mormon needs a vocabulary for at this point. 1830's plural 'bloodsheds' was singularized in 1920.

7:24.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: ‘the knowledge of the truth’ occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all in the Pastorals and Hebrews — 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7 and Hebrews 10:26. It is not an Old Testament idiom.
provenance.significance: The phrase is a late New Testament technical term for conversion, and the missionary purpose it names in 1 Timothy 2:4 — that all men be saved and come to it — is exactly what the Nephites' 'many means were devised' is trying to accomplish. Its appearance in a sixth-century BC narrative is the kind of availability failure this catalogue records rather than resolves.

7:24.note: 'Many means were devised, to reclaim and restore the Lamanites, to the knowledge of the truth.' Five words from a phrase confined to three KJV verses and to the latest stratum of the New Testament. Low, because the phrase is an idiom rather than a citation and no one of the three verses can be picked out; recorded because the idiom itself is the datum.
7:24.whyNot: Three occurrences with no distinguishing context means the source cannot be individuated, and a reader may reasonably treat 'knowledge of the truth' as ordinary religious English rather than a borrowing.

7:25.text: He shall cry unto me, Thou art my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation.

provenance.other: ‘rock of my salvation’ occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 89:26 and 2 Samuel 22:47; ‘God of the rock’ occurs in exactly one, 2 Samuel 22:47. 1830 reads 'the God and the rock of their salvation', which reproduces Psalm 89:26's article before 'rock'; 1920 deleted it, giving 'the God and rock of their salvation'.
provenance.significance: This is an 1830 reading that matters. The first edition's 'the God and the rock of their salvation' has the KJV's two articles and its conjunction, and stands one word away from Psalm 89:26; the 1920 correction tidied the English and moved the sentence away from its source. Psalm 89 is also apt in a way the psalm's title makes plain — it is the covenant psalm about the sure throne of David, quoted at the point where Jacob records that his people are so far holding out against their brethren.

7:25.note: 'Trusting in the God and the rock of their salvation.' The machine stream found this and ranked it first in the verse; the pairing of God with 'the rock of … salvation' has exactly two KJV homes, and 2 Samuel 22:47 supplies the additional 'God of the rock'. Recorded at moderate because the metaphor is a commonplace of the Psalter even where the exact phrase is not; the 1830 article is what makes the choice between Psalm 89:26 and the general idiom decidable.

7:26.text: For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.

provenance.other: ‘our days are passed away’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and ‘spend our years’ occurs in exactly one — the same verse. ‘a tale that is told’ occurs in exactly one. ‘fly away as a dream’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 20:8. James 4:14's 'what is your life? It is even a vapour' is the standing alternative and is answered below.
provenance.significance: Psalm 90 is the KJV's only psalm headed 'A Prayer of Moses the man of God', and Jacob's colophon — written by the man who has just spent a chapter defending himself against the charge of abandoning the law of Moses — closes his record in the psalm attributed to Moses. Recover the rest of it and the fit tightens: Psalm 90:10 makes a lifetime 'labour and sorrow', 90:15 asks God to gladden his people 'according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us', and the whole poem is a lament of a wandering generation that will not see the land. That is the sentence Jacob writes about his own people.
provenance.alternative: James 4:14 — 'what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away'. The figure is a life that vanishes and the machine stream reached it from 7:16; it is declined because Jacob's figure is a dream, not a vapour, and because Psalm 90:9 supplies the verb 'passed away' that the sentence actually repeats.

7:26.note: 'The time passed away with us, and also our lives passed away, like as it were unto us a dream … wherefore, we did mourn out our days.' Two of Psalm 90:9's clauses are KJV singletons and both are here in substance, with 'as a tale that is told' replaced by the dream figure of Job 20:8 — itself the KJV's only 'fly away as a dream'. The doubled 'passed away' is the psalm's verb used twice in one sentence, which is not how the phrase behaves elsewhere in the Book of Mormon.

7:26.text: My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations.

provenance.other: ‘wanderers’ occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 48:12 and Hosea 9:17. Only Hosea 9:17 joins the wandering to a casting-out, and it does so in one clause: cast away, therefore wanderers.
provenance.significance: Hosea's sentence is a judgment on Ephraim, and its logic is that exile follows from not hearkening. Jacob applies it to a people whose departure from Jerusalem the Book of Mormon has consistently presented as obedience rather than punishment — Lehi left because he did hearken — and yet the word he reaches for is the one Hosea uses for the disobedient cast out. The colophon's grief is the more legible for it: whatever the theology of the departure, the experience was Hosea's.

7:26.note: 'We being a lonesome and a solemn people, wanderers cast out from Jerusalem.' Both of Hosea 9:17's terms in Hosea's order, with 'among the nations' replaced by the place of origin. 'Lonesome' is not a KJV word at all, which is worth noticing: the biblical vocabulary supplies the condition and the nineteenth-century vocabulary supplies the feeling about it.

7:27.text: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.

provenance.other: ‘go down into the grave’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the speaker is Jacob. ‘my gray hairs’ — the same speaker's other formula for the same journey — occurs in exactly two, Genesis 42:38 and 44:29. The Book of Mormon has 'go down to my grave'; ‘down to the grave’ occurs in seven KJV verses, but none of them in the first person and none of them Jacob's.
provenance.significance: The patriarch Jacob is the only person in the King James Bible who says he will go down into the grave, and he says it three times, always mourning and always about his sons. Jacob the son of Lehi ends his book by saying it, one verse after telling the reader that his people were 'hated of our brethren' — which is Genesis 37:4-8's word for what Joseph's brothers did — and that 'we did mourn out our days', which is Genesis 37:34's mourning. The colophon is written in the voice of the man the writer is named for. Neither text says this; the coincidence of name, formula and grievance says it.

7:27.note: 'I, Jacob, saw that I must soon go down to my grave.' Five words of a formula the KJV gives to one speaker only, in a chapter that has already borrowed that speaker's mourning and his sons' hatred. The catalogue records this at high rather than certain because the wording is adjusted — 'to my grave' for 'into the grave' — and because a writer named Jacob might reach for Jacob's idiom without meaning an allusion. That, however, is the allusion.

7:27.text: Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.

provenance.other: ‘farewell’ occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Luke 9:61, Acts 18:21, Acts 23:30 and 2 Corinthians 13:11 — and only 2 Corinthians 13:11 uses it as a closing formula addressed to brethren. ‘the God of love and peace’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one.
provenance.significance: The last two things Jacob does are to bid the reader farewell and to address his brethren, which is 2 Corinthians 13:11's two-word closing in reverse order — and four verses earlier, at 7:23, the chapter has already reported that 'peace, and the love of God, was restored again among the people', which is the same verse's other half. A Pauline benediction is distributed across the end of the book: its blessing at 7:23, its sign-off at 7:27. The famous 'adieu' then sits where a KJV reader expects 'farewell', and is the one word in the sentence that is not from a Bible at all.

7:27.note: 'To the reader I bid farewell, hoping that many of my brethren may read my words. Brethren, adieu.' The KJV's four 'farewell's are answered here by two, and the only KJV closing formula that pairs the word with 'brethren' is 2 Corinthians 13:11. Recorded at moderate: 'farewell' is a natural English valediction and the argument depends on the pairing with 7:23 rather than on the word.
